opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was the right call, though I didn't feel that confident about it at the time.

When I was choosing, reinforcement learning was clearly the exciting thing, and Berkeley was one of the centers of it. Part of me worried I was walking away from the frontier. But looking back, what mattered most wasn't the topic I started on. It was the kind of training I got and the people I worked with day to day.

At CMU I had to build broader foundations. I spent a lot of time on the less glamorous parts: understanding the systems, thinking carefully about problem formulation, learning how to evaluate whether something actually works and isn't just a nice curve on one benchmark. That turned out to transfer really well. Research fields move so fast. What's hot when you apply is often not what's central four or five years later. If I had optimized purely for the trendiest area, I might have ended up very deep in one paradigm and less able to adapt.

And RL didn't disappear from my life. Those ideas come back everywhere now: in how we fine-tune large models, in decision-making, in agents. Coming at them from a slightly different angle actually helped me. I wasn't carrying all the assumptions of one school, so I could ask somewhat naive questions that sometimes turned out to be useful.

That said, I don't want to pretend there was no cost. There were moments when I watched work coming out of other labs and thought, "I could have been in that room." You do give something up. But I've come to believe the advisor fit, the environment, and whether you have room to develop your own taste matter much more than the label on the field. So if I had to make the decision again, I'd probably make the same one, just with less anxiety about it.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about it less as a right-or-wrong call and more as a bet on what kind of researcher I wanted to become. At the time, Berkeley was clearly the place for reinforcement learning, and I knew that. Staying there would have meant being in the center of the field, with the people and the infrastructure, and probably producing results faster early on.

But what drew me to CMU was the chance to work on problems that sat a bit outside that center. I wanted to spend time on the parts of the problem that reinforcement learning tends to assume away, like how you actually get a system to interact with a messy environment, how you deal with the hardware, the data, the engineering that makes any of this real. CMU had this culture where systems people, robotics people, and learning people were all in the same building, and I found that mix really valuable.

Looking back, I'd say it cost me something in the short term. I was slower to publish in the main reinforcement learning venues, and there were moments where I felt like I was watching the field move from the outside. But I also think it gave me a broader toolkit, and a healthier skepticism about which results actually transfer to the real world. A lot of the things I care about now came directly from that period of being a little off to the side.

So if I'm being fair, I'd judge it as the right decision for me, even if it wasn't the obvious one. It was a more uncomfortable path, and I'm not sure I would have had the patience for it if I'd fully understood how uncomfortable. But I don't think I'd trade it.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I don’t think there’s a clean way to say one path was better, because I only got to experience one of them. Berkeley would have meant working more directly on reinforcement learning, and that was appealing. But I wouldn’t judge the decision to go to CMU only by how closely it matched that interest at the time. A PhD is also about learning how to choose problems and developing your own judgment as a researcher. So I’d separate whether it was a reasonable decision then from whether I can prove today that it was the best possible choice. The second question is much harder to answer.

That’s the lens I’d use to judge the decision, rather than whether I picked the right research area at that particular moment.
